title: Why the Austin boys became musicians and Ashcraft did not
summary: Ashcraft explains his law-school path versus the Austin boys, their fathers, Chicago's Capone-era joints, union scale and a Ben Bernie offer.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: All right. Then let's go back a little earlier if we can. Do you remember that these fellows had reason to look to music as a permanent livelihood? The call for musicians was growing, wasn't it? They could work five nights. Yeah. And they could work their summers and it was fairly pleasant work. Did the decision arise because they recognized their talent or did it arise because they enjoyed the music so much? What do you suppose was behind the Chicago boys deciding to become musicians? You didn't but you must have known something about their feeling.

Yes, I did. I was in a sort of a different economic bracket in a way. That was one reason. Another was I was predestined for college and law school. And I had an extremely strong-willed father who, that was, let's say, half the reason. I think the other half was the fact that I didn't feel that I was very talented at all. In the case of the Austin boys, they didn't, as a rule, have any definite profession to go into or any particular thing that they were aiming at. I would say that because they loved it so much and they were as dedicated as you can be as a teenager to something like that, that the way for them to drift into it in the face of this increased. In the face of this increasing demand for musicians was easy. It was a line of least resistance. I don't doubt whatsoever that Jimmy McPartland's father put up an awful battle about the two of them going into it. I'm quite sure he did.
Well, yet he was a musician, wasn't he?

Yes, he was. But I don't think he wanted them to do that particularly. It was like Jimmy Dorsey's father. I mean, he didn't want them to get into it, although I think he started both of them on trumpet.
Probably in both cases, the fathers didn't realize that music might develop to the economic security that it did for a long period at any rate.

It's still, in Chicago, it didn't have the connotations it did in New Orleans about the places where you worked, the Storyville type, for instance. It was, it, but they still were, it still was a Capone town, if you remember.

And the, the, the joints were joints and there was no other way of describing them. Some of them were fancier than others, but you were still working, uh, for what was then a pretty darn good rate of pay. I'm not sure whether Petrillo was in them, but the, but the, the, the, the white union was, was pretty effective. And in its interest in getting the weight scale up for the pit bands, which is all it was really concerned with, the large mass of fiddle players, it managed to get the scale up so much that it was very tempting. It was for me when I got out of college. The, I had a, uh, Ben Burney wanted me to play accordion with him, uh, on a five-year contract at 150 a week. Didn't, uh, this is 29.
